propositions.text: Whether self-induced intoxication is a defence to arson under s. 434 of the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: This case requires the Court to determine whether self-induced intoxication is a defence to a charge of arson under s. 434 of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 .

propositions.text: The charge against Mr. Tatton arose from a fire he caused while intoxicated.
propositions.quote: The charge against the respondent, Mr. Tatton, arose out of a fire that destroyed the contents of his ex-girlfriend’s home.

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton placed oil on stove, set burner to high, left to get coffee, and returned to find the house on fire.
propositions.quote: The fire began after Mr. Tatton, in a highly intoxicated state, placed a pan with oil on the stove, set the burner to “high”, and left the house to get a coffee at a nearby Tim Hortons. When he returned approximately 20 minutes later, the house was on fire.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the issue is whether self-induced intoxication is a defence to arson under s. 434, describing Mr. Tatton's intoxicated actions causing the fire.

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton sought to rely on accident defence based on drunkenness to rebut intent for arson.
propositions.quote: At trial, Mr. Tatton sought to rely on the defence of accident based on his drunkenness to rebut the intent required for the offence of arson.

propositions.text: Trial judge found Mr. Tatton could rely on intoxication defence; majority of Court of Appeal agreed.
propositions.quote: The trial judge found that he could do so, and a majority of the Court of Appeal agreed.

propositions.text: Trial judge and majority of Court of Appeal erred; intoxication short of automatism is not a defence to arson under s. 434.
propositions.quote: For reasons that follow, I am respectfully of the view that the trial judge and the majority of the Court of Appeal erred. Intoxication short of automatism is not a defence to a charge of arson under s. 434 of the Criminal Code .

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argued intoxication was a defence; trial judge and Court of Appeal agreed, but the Court finds this was an error.

propositions.text: In September 2010, Mr. Tatton lived in a guest room at ex-girlfriend Ms. Spencer's home after their breakup.
propositions.quote: In September 2010, Mr. Tatton was living in a guest room at a home owned by his ex-girlfriend, Ms. Spencer. He and Ms. Spencer had broken off their relationship, but Mr. Tatton remained hopeful that they would reconcile.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Tatton lived in his ex-girlfriend's home after their breakup, hoping to reconcile.

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton was an alcoholic with binge drinking, blackouts, and memory loss while intoxicated.
propositions.quote: Mr. Tatton was an alcoholic. He had a tendency to binge drink. There was evidence that in the past he had come home drunk, started to cook food, and then passed out, only to awake to a house filled with smoke. His history with alcoholism included periods of blackouts. He would sometimes have no recollection of events that had transpired while he was under the influence of alcohol.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Tatton had a history of alcoholism, binge drinking, blackouts, and memory loss when intoxicated.

propositions.text: On Sept 24, 2010, Mr. Tatton drank heavily, left agitated messages to Ms. Spencer, and passed out.
propositions.quote: On September 24, 2010, Ms. Spencer went to Kingston to visit friends. Mr. Tatton was not happy about this and became jealous and upset. He drank heavily throughout the day and evening, consuming approximately 52 ounces of alcohol. Over the course of the evening, he left Ms. Spencer a series of agitated voice messages on her cell phone, two of which referred to her home being on fire. Eventually, Mr. Tatton passed out.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Tatton drank heavily, left agitated messages about fire, and passed out on Sept 24, 2010.

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton cooked bacon with oil on stove set to high, left for coffee, returned to find house on fire, called 911, and apologized next day.
propositions.quote: When Mr. Tatton awoke, he decided to cook some bacon. He put some vegetable oil in a pan on the stove and set the temperature to “high”. He then drove to a nearby Tim Hortons to get a coffee. When he returned 15-20 minutes later, the house was on fire. Mr. Tatton called 911 from a neighbouring house. The firefighters were able to save the home, but not its contents. The next day, Mr. Tatton left Ms. Spencer a message apologizing for the incident and stating that it was an accident.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Tatton set stove high with oil, left for coffee, returned to fire, called 911, and apologized as accident next day.

propositions.text: Fire investigator found fire source was vegetable oil on stove; Mr. Tatton charged with arson under s. 434.
propositions.quote: The fire investigator determined that the source of the fire was the vegetable oil on the stove. Mr. Tatton was arrested and charged with arson contrary to s. 434 of the Criminal Code .

propositions.text: Section 434 defines arson as intentionally or recklessly causing fire damage to property not wholly owned by the person, punishable by up to 14 years.
propositions.quote: 434. Every person who intentionally or recklessly causes damage by fire or explosion to property that is not wholly owned by that person is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years.

paragraphs.summary: Fire was caused by oil on stove; Mr. Tatton charged with arson under s. 434, which punishes intentional or reckless fire damage.

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton claimed fire was accident; he thought stove was set to low and did not intend or foresee damage.
propositions.quote: At trial, Mr. Tatton claimed that the fire was an accident. When he put the oil on the stove, he thought he had set the temperature at “low”. He did not intend or foresee the consequences that resulted from his turning the stove on and leaving it unattended.

propositions.text: Central trial question was whether Mr. Tatton had requisite intent for arson and if intoxication could be considered.
propositions.quote: A central question at trial was whether Mr. Tatton had the requisite intent to commit the offence of arson under s. 434 , and more particularly whether the court could take his state of intoxication into account in making its assessment.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Tatton claimed accident due to mistaken stove setting; trial focused on intent and role of intoxication.

propositions.text: Trial judge found s. 434 a specific intent offence, allowing intoxication defence, and acquitted Mr. Tatton.
propositions.quote: The trial judge determined that s. 434 was a specific intent offence, meaning that Mr. Tatton could rely on self-induced intoxication as a defence. In the end, he acquitted Mr. Tatton because he was not convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Tatton intentionally or recklessly left the stove on “high”.

propositions.text: Majority of Court of Appeal upheld acquittal; one member dissented and would have ordered new trial.
propositions.quote: A majority of the Court of Appeal for Ontario upheld Mr. Tatton’s acquittal. The third member of the panel would have allowed the appeal and ordered a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge and majority of Court of Appeal found s. 434 specific intent offence, acquitted Mr. Tatton; dissent wanted new trial.

propositions.text: Crown appeals arguing arson under s. 434 is general intent offence; intoxication short of automatism not relevant.
propositions.quote: The Crown appeals to this Court as of right. It argues that arson contrary to s. 434 is a general intent offence, meaning that intoxication falling short of automatism cannot be considered.

propositions.text: Court agrees arson under s. 434 is general intent offence; trial judge's error requires new trial.
propositions.quote: I agree. I further agree that a new trial is required because the trial judge’s critical findings of fact were tainted by his belief that self-induced intoxication was relevant to the issue of intent. Accordingly, I would allow the appeal, set aside the verdict of acquittal, and order a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: Crown appeals that arson is general intent offence; Court agrees and orders new trial due to trial judge's error.

propositions.text: Live issue at trial was whether Mr. Tatton caused fire intentionally or recklessly to infer intent for arson.
propositions.quote: The only live issue before the trial judge was whether Mr. Tatton had caused the fire intentionally or recklessly. If so, it could be inferred, in the circumstances, that in setting the fire he either intended to cause damage to the contents of the home or was reckless whether damage ensued or not.

propositions.text: If fire was accidental or negligent, intent for arson could not be inferred.
propositions.quote: On the other hand, if the fire started by reason of accident or negligence, then it could not be inferred that Mr. Tatton had one of the intents required to support a conviction under s. 434 .

paragraphs.summary: Trial issue was whether fire was intentional or reckless to infer arson intent; accident or negligence negated intent inference.

propositions.text: Trial judge found Mr. Tatton heavily intoxicated and needed to determine if arson was specific or general intent offence.
propositions.quote: The trial judge found that Mr. Tatton was heavily under the influence of alcohol at the time of the fire. Consequently, he held that it was necessary to determine whether arson was a crime of specific or general intent.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found heavy intoxication and needed to classify arson as specific or general intent offence.

propositions.text: Trial judge concluded classification of s. 434 as general or specific intent was fact-driven, depending on how fire started.
propositions.quote: The trial judge concluded that the characterization of s. 434 as either an offence of general or specific intent was fact-driven. In his view, the proper characterization depended on how the fire started.

propositions.text: If fire started by match and combustible, arson likely general intent; if nuanced, could be specific intent.
propositions.quote: If an accused started a fire with a match and combustible material, the charge of arson would likely be one of general intent. However, if the way in which the fire started was more nuanced, it could be a specific intent offence.

propositions.text: On facts, trial judge found offence specific intent, allowing intoxication defence, and acquitted Mr. Tatton.
propositions.quote: On the facts before him, the trial judge found that the offence was one of specific intent, such that Mr. Tatton’s state of intoxication could be considered. In the end, he was not “satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that [Mr. Tatton] left the setting [on the stove] on ‘high’ either intentionally or recklessly”: A.R., vol. I, at p. 81. Accordingly, he acquitted Mr. Tatton on the charge of arson.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found s. 434 classification fact-driven, deemed offence specific intent, allowed intoxication defence, acquitted Mr. Tatton.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal unanimously rejected trial judge's fact-driven classification of s. 434; classification is a question of law.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal unanimously rejected the trial judge’s conclusion that the characterization of s. 434 as an offence of general or specific intent was fact-driven and dependent on how the fire started. Rather, the court determined — correctly in my view — that the characterization of s. 434 amounted to a question of law.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal divided on classification question.
propositions.quote: On that question, the court divided.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal rejected fact-driven classification, held s. 434 classification is legal question, but court divided on classification.

propositions.text: Majority (Pardu J.A.) characterized arson under s. 434 as specific intent offence requiring voluntary act and awareness of consequences.
propositions.quote: Writing for the majority, Pardu J.A. characterized arson under s. 434 as a specific intent offence. In her view, s. 434 required a voluntary act, coupled with an awareness of the more distant consequences of that act, and a decision to proceed in the face of those consequences.

propositions.text: Many household activities cause fires but do not imply intentional or reckless damage; intoxication not significant cause of household fires.
propositions.quote: Justice Pardu noted that many ordinary household activities cause fires; however, they do not lead inevitably to the conclusion that the person intentionally or recklessly damaged property. Furthermore, there was no basis to conclude that intoxication played a significant role in causing household fires.

paragraphs.summary: Majority of Court of Appeal found s. 434 specific intent offence requiring awareness; intoxication not significant cause of household fires.

propositions.text: Majority held if arson were general intent, mens rea would be objective; words 'intentionally or recklessly' require subjective mens rea relevant to intoxication.
propositions.quote: Justice Pardu also maintained that if arson were to be characterized as a general intent offence, the mens rea for the offence would be objective, not subjective. In her view, the words “intentionally or recklessly” require consideration of an accused’s subjective state of mind, to which intoxication is relevant.

propositions.text: Majority found s. 434 specific intent offence and upheld Mr. Tatton’s acquittal.
propositions.quote: Consequently, she found that s. 434 was a specific intent offence, and upheld Mr. Tatton’s acquittal.

paragraphs.summary: Majority reasoned s. 434 requires subjective mens rea, thus specific intent offence, and upheld acquittal.

propositions.text: Dissent (Goudge J.A.) concluded s. 434 is general intent offence; intoxication short of automatism not relevant.
propositions.quote: In dissent, Goudge J.A. concluded that s. 434 was a general intent offence and that intoxication short of automatism could therefore not be considered.

propositions.text: Dissent held mens rea does not extend beyond actus reus; no ulterior purpose required.
propositions.quote: He held that the mens rea for s. 434 did not extend beyond the actus reus, and that no ulterior purpose was required.

propositions.text: Dissent argued arson is offence people commit when intoxicated; policy reasons to refuse intoxication defence.
propositions.quote: He was also of the view that arson is the type of offence that people are apt to commit when intoxicated; therefore, there were good policy reasons for refusing to allow an accused to raise the defence of self-induced intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: Dissent found s. 434 general intent offence, mens rea limited to actus reus, and policy supports refusing intoxication defence.

propositions.text: Dissent disagreed that excluding intoxication makes mens rea objective; inquiry remains subjective to accused's sober foresight.
propositions.quote: Justice Goudge disagreed with the majority that precluding reliance on intoxication transformed the mens rea inquiry into an objective one. In his view, the inquiry does not ask if a reasonable person would have foreseen the risk of damage to property; rather, one asks if the particular accused, while sober, would have foreseen the risk.

propositions.text: Dissent concluded s. 434 not specific intent offence; trial judge erred and error materially affected outcome; new trial warranted.
propositions.quote: It followed that arson under s. 434 was not a specific intent offence and that the trial judge erred in concluding otherwise. Justice Goudge held that the error had a material bearing on the outcome. Hence, he would have ordered a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: Dissent held mens rea inquiry remains subjective without intoxication defence; s. 434 not specific intent; trial judge erred; new trial needed.

propositions.text: Two issues on appeal: classification of arson under s. 434 as general or specific intent; and if general intent, whether trial judge's error materially affected verdict.
propositions.quote: There are two issues on appeal: 1. Is arson contrary to s. 434 a general or specific intent offence? 2. If arson contrary to s. 434 is a general intent offence, did the trial judge’s error have a material bearing on the verdict?

paragraphs.summary: Court states two appeal issues: classification of arson as general or specific intent, and materiality of trial judge's error if general intent.

propositions.text: Classification as general or specific intent affects accused; self-induced intoxication short of automatism not defence for general intent offences.
propositions.quote: The classification of an offence as one involving general or specific intent has important consequences for the accused. The law does not allow offenders to rely on self-induced intoxication falling short of automatism as an excuse for general intent offences: R. v. Daviault, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 63, at p. 123; R. v. Bernard, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 833, at pp. 865 and 878-80.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains classification of offences affects intoxication defence; intoxication short of automatism not defence for general intent offences.

propositions.text: General and specific intent labels are entrenched but unhelpful for describing the mental element of a crime.
propositions.quote: Although the labels “general intent” and “specific intent” are entrenched in Canadian law, they are not particularly helpful in describing the actual mental element required for a crime

propositions.text: The distinction lies in the complexity of thought and reasoning processes and the social policy underlying the offence.
propositions.quote: the distinction lies in the complexity of the thought and reasoning processes that make up the mental element of a particular offence, and the social policy underlying the offence

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that general and specific intent labels are entrenched but unhelpful; the distinction lies in complexity of thought and social policy.

propositions.text: Daviault is the leading case on general and specific intent but has not resolved confusion.
propositions.quote: This Court’s decision in Daviault is the leading case on the distinction between general and specific intent crimes. Unfortunately, it has not resolved the confusion surrounding this issue.

propositions.text: The general/specific intent dichotomy is criticized as illogical and inconsistent across courts and jurisdictions.
propositions.quote: The general/specific intent dichotomy continues to perplex counsel and trial courts alike. It has been criticized as illogical and as leading to “arbitrary and inconsistent results from court to court, offence to offence and jurisdiction to jurisdiction”

paragraphs.summary: The court states Daviault is leading but confusing; prior authorities criticize the general/specific intent dichotomy as illogical and inconsistent.

propositions.text: The Criminal Code often lacks clear direction on the mental element, leaving judges to divine the fault requirement.
propositions.quote: the Criminal Code often provides no clear direction about the required mental element for a given offence. It is therefore left to judges to attempt to divine the required mental element

propositions.text: Professor Stuart states confusion on fault requirement undermines legitimacy of adversary system and presumption of innocence.
propositions.quote: Our adversary system, which requires cases to be fairly put to impartial judges or juries, and the presumption of innocence, cannot work with legitimacy where there is confusion as to the applicable tests on even basic matters such as the fault requirement

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Criminal Code lacks clear mental element guidance; Stuart says this confusion undermines legitimacy of the justice system.

propositions.text: Scholars and law reform bodies urge amending the Criminal Code to specify mental elements and fault requirements for each crime.
propositions.quote: He and other academics and law reform bodies have urged that the Criminal Code be amended to specify the mental element and fault requirement for each crime

paragraphs.summary: The court reports scholars and reformers urge Criminal Code amendments to clarify mental elements and fault requirements.

propositions.text: The difficulty in classifying offences as general or specific intent stems from unclear mental element requirements.
propositions.quote: The shortcoming identified by Professor Stuart and other scholars is the source of the difficulty in determining whether an offence is one of general or specific intent

propositions.text: Legislative intervention is needed to clarify mental elements and intoxication defences, but the existing regime remains.
propositions.quote: Legislative intervention is sorely needed to spell out the mental element of offences and to specify when intoxication short of automatism can be considered. However, until that day comes we are left with the existing regime

propositions.text: Before classifying s. 434 offence, the court will review Daviault analysis to clarify the general/specific intent distinction.
propositions.quote: before turning to the proper classification of the offence in s. 434 of the Criminal Code , I propose to review the analysis in Daviault in the hope of shedding a bit more light on the general/specific intent distinction

paragraphs.summary: The court finds unclear mental elements cause classification difficulty; legislative reform is needed but the court will review Daviault first.

propositions.text: Daviault examined whether extreme intoxication akin to automatism can be a defence to general intent crimes.
propositions.quote: In Daviault, this Court examined whether an accused who is in a state of extreme intoxication, akin to automatism, may rely on drunkenness as a defence to a general intent crime

propositions.text: Sopinka J. held two factors distinguish general from specific intent crimes: nature and importance of mental element, and social policy.
propositions.quote: He held that two factors help distinguish crimes of general intent from those of specific intent: first, “[t]he nature of the mental element and its relative importance” and second, “the social policy sought to be attained by criminalizing the particular conduct”

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Daviault examined intoxication defence; Sopinka J. identified mental element nature and social policy as distinguishing factors.

propositions.text: General intent crimes involve minimal intent to do the act constituting the actus reus.
propositions.quote: Justice Sopinka specified that general intent crimes involve “the minimal intent to do the act which constitutes the actus reus”

propositions.text: Minimal thought means intoxication short of automatism unlikely to negate required mental element for general intent crimes.
propositions.quote: even a high degree of intoxication short of automatism is unlikely to deprive the accused of the slight degree of mental acuity required to commit them

propositions.text: Allowing intoxication defence for general intent crimes contradicts social policy because drunk persons are apt to commit these offences.
propositions.quote: general intent crimes tend to be “offences that persons who are drunk are apt to commit”... allowing intoxication to operate as a defence would contradict the social policy underlying these crimes

paragraphs.summary: Sopinka J. found general intent crimes require minimal intent; intoxication short of automatism unlikely negates this; intoxication defence contradicts social policy.

propositions.text: Specific intent crimes require a heightened mental element involving further ulterior motives and purposes.
propositions.quote: specific intent crimes require a heightened mental element. For example, they often require “the formation of further ulterior motives and purposes”

propositions.text: Intoxication short of automatism may negate the mental element for specific intent crimes.
propositions.quote: one can readily understand how intoxication short of automatism may negate the required mental element

propositions.text: Specific intent offences are less likely to be committed by intoxicated persons, so policy against intoxication defence is less pressing.
propositions.quote: specific intent offences are less likely to be the type of offences that intoxicated people are apt to commit. For that reason, policy considerations that might otherwise militate against a defence of intoxication are less pressing

paragraphs.summary: Sopinka J. held specific intent crimes require heightened mental element; intoxication may negate it; policy against intoxication defence is less pressing.

propositions.text: Specific intent offences often include lesser general intent offences, so intoxicated offenders may still be punished.
propositions.quote: specific intent offences often include lesser offences that only require general intent. In such cases, an intoxicated offender will not escape punishment altogether

paragraphs.summary: Sopinka J. noted specific intent offences often include lesser general intent offences, so intoxicated offenders may still be punished.

propositions.text: Classification of offence as general or specific intent starts with determining the mental element by statutory interpretation.
propositions.quote: The analysis of whether an offence is one of specific or general intent must start with a determination of the mental element of the offence in question. This is an exercise in statutory interpretation

propositions.text: This determination should not be a factual assessment based on case circumstances.
propositions.quote: Care should be taken not to turn it into a factual assessment based on the circumstances of the particular case

paragraphs.summary: The court rules classification starts with statutory interpretation of mental element, not factual assessment of case circumstances.

propositions.text: The general/specific intent distinction is not precise; logic, intuition, and policy all play a part.
propositions.quote: The distinction between general and specific intent offences is not a precise science. Logic, intuition, and policy all play a part

propositions.text: The task is formidable for criminal law experts and daunting for others.
propositions.quote: The task has proved formidable to those who have been schooled in criminal law, and daunting to those who have not

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the general/specific intent distinction imprecise, involving logic, intuition, and policy, and is difficult even for experts.

propositions.text: If jurisprudence has classified an offence satisfactorily, that classification should be followed.
propositions.quote: Where the jurisprudence has already determined the appropriate classification of the offence in a satisfactory manner, the task is straightforward

propositions.text: Sexual assault is general intent; robbery and murder are specific intent offences per established cases.
propositions.quote: this Court has established that sexual assault is a general intent offence, whereas robbery and murder are specific intent offences

propositions.text: If jurisprudence is unclear, courts must examine Daviault factors to classify the offence.
propositions.quote: if the jurisprudence is unclear, courts must examine the factors outlined in Daviault, as clarified below, to resolve the question

propositions.text: The framework clarifies but does not change Daviault law.
propositions.quote: The framework that follows is meant to clarify, not change the law as set out in Daviault

paragraphs.summary: The court rules to follow established jurisprudence classifications; if unclear, apply Daviault factors; framework clarifies but does not change law.

propositions.text: Daviault identified two main considerations: importance of mental element and social policy, but left questions unanswered.
propositions.quote: Daviault made clear that there are two main considerations when determining if intoxication short of automatism can be considered — the “importance” of the mental element, and the social policy underlying the offence — it left certain questions unanswered

propositions.text: Questions remain about the meaning of 'importance' of mental element and when policy considerations apply.
propositions.quote: it provided no clear explanation of what is meant by the “importance” of the mental element. Second, it did not specify whether policy considerations should always play a role in the analysis or whether they should only come into play if an examination of the mental element left unclear how the offence should be characterized

propositions.text: The court will address these questions to clarify the law.
propositions.quote: I turn to these questions in the hope of bringing some added clarity to an area of the law that continues to perplex and confound

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Daviault left unclear the meaning of 'importance' and role of policy; the court will clarify these issues.

propositions.text: Daviault's 'importance' of mental element refers to complexity of thought and reasoning processes.
propositions.quote: it is clear that he was referring to the complexity of the thought and reasoning processes that make up the mental element of a particular offence

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Daviault's 'importance' means complexity of thought and reasoning in the mental element.

propositions.text: General intent crimes require intent to do the act but not intent to cause external consequences or actual knowledge requiring complex reasoning.
propositions.quote: For general intent crimes, the mental element simply relates to the performance of an illegal act... Such crimes do not require an intent to bring about certain consequences that are external to the actus reus

propositions.text: Assault is a classic general intent crime requiring intentional force but not intent to cause injury.
propositions.quote: Assault is a classic example. The accused must intentionally apply force; however, there is no requirement that he intend to cause injury

propositions.text: General intent crimes do not require actual knowledge of circumstances or consequences involving complex reasoning.
propositions.quote: crimes of general intent do not require actual knowledge of certain circumstances or consequences, to the extent that such knowledge is the product of complex thought and reasoning processes

paragraphs.summary: The court finds general intent crimes require intent to do the act but not intent to cause consequences or complex knowledge; assault is an example.

propositions.text: 'Straightforward' mental element means minimal intent and minimal degree of consciousness as in Daviault.
propositions.quote: I am using these phrases synonymously with the descriptors used in Daviault: “minimal intent” and “minimal degree of consciousness”

paragraphs.summary: The court clarifies 'straightforward' mental element means minimal intent and consciousness as per Daviault.

propositions.text: Specific intent crimes require an ulterior purpose beyond the actus reus, e.g., assault with intent to resist arrest.
propositions.quote: For such crimes, the accused must not only intend to do the act that constitutes the actus reus, he must also act with an ulterior purpose in mind

paragraphs.summary: The court finds specific intent crimes require an ulterior purpose beyond the act, such as assault with intent to resist arrest.

propositions.text: A heightened mental element may also require intent to cause consequences or actual knowledge involving complex reasoning, not just ulterior purpose.
propositions.quote: a heightened mental element could take the form of a requirement that the accused intend and bring about certain consequences, if the formation of that intent involves more complex thought and reasoning processes

propositions.text: Possession of stolen property requires actual knowledge or willful blindness, making intoxication defence available.
propositions.quote: Possession of stolen property is one such crime. The accused must actually know or be willfully blind to the fact that the goods he or she possesses are stolen... Intoxication is therefore available as a defence for such crimes

paragraphs.summary: The court finds heightened mental element may require intent to cause consequences or knowledge; possession of stolen property requires knowledge, allowing intoxication defence.

propositions.text: Specific intent offences have heightened mental elements involving ulterior purpose, knowledge, or intent to cause consequences with complex reasoning.
propositions.quote: specific intent offences contain a heightened mental element. That element may take the form of an ulterior purpose or it may entail actual knowledge of certain circumstances or consequences

propositions.text: General intent offences require very little mental acuity.
propositions.quote: General intent offences, on the other hand, require very little mental acuity

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes specific intent offences require heightened mental elements; general intent offences require little mental acuity.

propositions.text: Daviault left unclear when policy considerations should be considered in classifying offences.
propositions.quote: The second question that Daviault left unanswered is the stage at which policy ought to be considered

propositions.text: Confusion exists whether policy should always be considered or only if mental element analysis is unclear.
propositions.quote: Confusion remains about whether policy should be considered in every case or whether it should only come into play if an examination of the mental element leaves it unclear how the offence should be characterized

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies confusion about when policy considerations apply in offence classification after mental element analysis.

propositions.text: First examine the nature of the mental element before considering policy in intoxication defence analysis.
propositions.quote: In my view, the most logical approach is to first examine the nature of the mental element. Only when this analysis fails to yield a clear answer should one turn to policy considerations.

propositions.text: Daviault explains policy is tied to mental element; general intent crimes have minimal mental acuity making intoxication defence unavailable.
propositions.quote: As Daviault explains, policy considerations are closely tied to the nature of the mental element. General intent crimes involve such minimal mental acuity that it is difficult to see how intoxication short of automatism could deprive the accused of the low level of intent required.

propositions.text: It is constitutionally permissible to deny intoxication defence for general intent offences.
propositions.quote: This provides a strong policy reason for precluding reliance on intoxication for these offences: Daviault, at p. 123. It also explains why it is constitutionally permissible to render the intoxication defence unavailable for general intent offences: ibid., at pp. 99-100.

propositions.text: Specific intent crimes require complex thought and intoxication may negate that, so intoxication defence can be considered.
propositions.quote: In contrast, one can more readily understand how the more complex thought and reasoning processes required for specific intent crimes may be negated by an accused’s intoxication. For that reason, policy suggests that intoxication can be considered for specific intent crimes.

propositions.text: If mental element analysis clearly characterizes offence, policy considerations are unnecessary.
propositions.quote: Thus, if an examination of the mental element clearly indicates how the offence should be characterized, there is little reason to resort to policy considerations.

paragraphs.summary: The court states mental element should be examined first; intoxication defence is unavailable for general intent crimes but may be for specific intent; policy is intertwined with mental element.

propositions.text: If mental element analysis is unclear, policy considerations may resolve intoxication defence availability.
propositions.quote: However, if an examination of the mental element does not provide a clear answer, policy considerations may help resolve the question.

propositions.text: Policy focuses on whether alcohol consumption is habitually associated with the crime.
propositions.quote: In the main, the policy assessment will focus on whether alcohol consumption is habitually associated with the crime in question.

propositions.text: Allowing intoxication defence for crimes habitually linked to alcohol is counterintuitive and promotes problematic behaviour.
propositions.quote: Allowing self-induced intoxication to provide an accused with a defence would be to endorse, if not promote, the very behaviour that has historically proved to be a root cause of the problem.

propositions.text: Law and common sense should not diverge; where intoxication rarely plays a role, denying intoxication defence makes less policy sense.
propositions.quote: By the same token, where self-induced intoxication rarely, if ever, plays a role in the commission of a particular crime, preventing an accused from relying on it makes less sense from a policy perspective.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains policy considerations apply if mental element is unclear, focusing on habitual alcohol association with the crime and policy implications of allowing intoxication defence.

propositions.text: Alcohol often plays a role in violent or unruly conduct and property damage crimes, so intoxication defence is generally inappropriate.
propositions.quote: As a general observation, and without setting out a general rule, alcohol habitually plays a role in crimes involving violent or unruly conduct: Bernard, at p. 880. It also tends to be prevalent in crimes involving damage to property.

propositions.text: It makes little policy sense that intoxication should provide a defence for crimes harming people or property.
propositions.quote: As such, it makes little sense from a policy perspective that it should provide a defence for crimes in which people or property are harmed or endangered: Daviault, at p. 123.

propositions.text: Murder is a specific intent crime with intoxication defence available due to complex reasoning, gravity, punishment, and lesser included offence.
propositions.quote: Murder, for example, has long been considered a crime of specific intent for which the defence of intoxication is available. As Daviault explains, at p. 124, this is a function of the heightened thought and reasoning processes required, the gravity of the offence, the serious fixed punishment upon conviction, and the availability of the lesser included offence of manslaughter.

propositions.text: It is incorrect to say intoxication is never considered in violent or property damage crimes, but policy reasons often oppose intoxication defence.
propositions.quote: It is therefore incorrect to state that intoxication may never be considered in crimes involving violence against people or damage to property. However, given the prevalence of alcohol in these crimes, there are likely to be strong policy reasons militating against an intoxication-based defence.

paragraphs.summary: The court observes alcohol's role in violent and property crimes, notes murder as a specific intent exception, and states policy often opposes intoxication defence in such crimes.

propositions.text: Presence of lesser included general intent offence may allow intoxication defence for main offence as lesser offence conviction remains possible.
propositions.quote: As noted in Daviault, the presence of a lesser included general intent offence in the main offence may be relevant. In such cases, an accused who successfully relies on intoxication to negate the heightened mental element of the main offence can still be convicted of the lesser included offence.

propositions.text: Drunkenness provides no defence to lesser offence, so intoxicated offender won't escape punishment entirely.
propositions.quote: Drunkenness will provide no defence to the lesser offence. For example, an accused who successfully raises intoxication as a defence to a charge of assault with intent to resist arrest may still be convicted of the lesser included offence of assault.

propositions.text: Less reason to preclude intoxication defence for main offence when lesser offence conviction remains possible.
propositions.quote: Consequently, there is less impetus to preclude the accused from advancing intoxication as a defence to the main offence.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that when a lesser included general intent offence exists, intoxication defence for the main offence is less likely to be precluded.

propositions.text: Judicial sentencing discretion may affect whether intoxication defence should be precluded.
propositions.quote: In addition, the presence of judicial sentencing discretion may be a factor to consider.

propositions.text: If heavy minimum sentence applies, precluding intoxication defence may be harsh; if judge can tailor sentence considering intoxication, preclusion is less worrisome.
propositions.quote: If the crime is one for which the accused will receive a heavy minimum sentence upon conviction, it may be unduly harsh to preclude consideration of intoxication. However, if the judge has discretion to tailor the sentence to the facts of the case and to consider the accused’s intoxication as part of that assessment, precluding the accused from advancing a defence of intoxication is less worrisome: Daviault, at p. 124.

paragraphs.summary: The court states judicial sentencing discretion may influence whether intoxication defence should be allowed, citing Daviault on sentencing and intoxication.

propositions.text: Arson offence in s. 434 has a long history with courts divided on whether it is general or specific intent.
propositions.quote: The crime of arson has existed for many years, and the Criminal Code provisions have gone through many iterations. Over the years, courts have been divided on whether the offence of arson in s. 434 (and its predecessors) is a crime of general or specific intent: see, e.g., R. v. Swanson (1989), 48 C.C.C. (3d) 316 (Y.T.C.A.) (specific intent); R. v. Hudson (1993), 88 Man. R. (2d) 150 (C.A.) (specific intent); and R. v. Muma (1989), 51 C.C.C. (3d) 85 (Ont. C.A.) (general intent), relying on R. v. Schmidtke (1985), 19 C.C.C. (3d) 390 (Ont. C.A.).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes courts have been divided on whether s. 434 arson is general or specific intent offence.

propositions.text: Section 434 arson is a general intent offence; intoxication short of automatism is not a defence.
propositions.quote: Applying the framework outlined above to the offence of arson in s. 434 , I am satisfied that s. 434 is a general intent offence for which intoxication falling short of automatism is not available as a defence.

propositions.text: Section 434 provision states intentional or reckless damage by fire to property not wholly owned by person is indictable offence.
propositions.quote: For convenience, I repeat the provision: 434. Every person who intentionally or recklessly causes damage by fire or explosion to property that is not wholly owned by that person is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 434 arson is a general intent offence without intoxication defence and repeats the statutory provision.

propositions.text: Actus reus is damaging property by fire; mental element is intentional or reckless causing of damage; no complex reasoning needed.
propositions.quote: The actus reus is the damaging of property by fire. The mental element is the intentional or reckless performance of the illegal act — the causing of damage to property. No additional knowledge or purpose is needed. No complex thought or reasoning processes are required.

propositions.text: Level of intent required for s. 434 appears minimal.
propositions.quote: On its face, the level of intent required for the offence would appear to be minimal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 434 requires minimal intent: intentional or reckless damage by fire without complex reasoning.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal majority worried that classifying s. 434 as general intent would make recklessness an objective inquiry.
propositions.quote: A majority of the Court of Appeal was concerned that if s. 434 were found to be a general intent offence, so as to preclude consideration of intoxication short of automatism, that would improperly transform the examination of recklessness into an objective inquiry.

propositions.text: Court disagrees; recklessness is subjective, involving awareness of risk and disregard for consequences.
propositions.quote: With respect, I cannot agree. Recklessness describes the act of one who sees the risk and acts without regard for the consequences: Sansregret v. The Queen, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 570, at p. 582. It always involves a subjective inquiry — and this case is no exception.

propositions.text: Arson under s. 434 does not involve sophisticated reasoning; risk of damage by fire is typically obvious.
propositions.quote: However, the offence of arson under s. 434 does not involve sophisticated reasoning. The risk of damage by fire is typically obvious, even when it involves a chain of events and not the simple application of a match to the property in question.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects Court of Appeal's concern that recklessness would become objective, affirming recklessness is subjective and risk obvious in s. 434 arson.

propositions.text: Intoxication short of automatism unlikely to prevent accused from foreseeing risk of property damage by fire.
propositions.quote: I have difficulty seeing how intoxication short of automatism would prevent an accused from foreseeing the risk of causing damage to someone else’s property by fire.

propositions.text: Precluding intoxication defence does not make recklessness objective but recognizes minimal intent remains despite intoxication.
propositions.quote: Thus, preventing an accused from advancing the defence of intoxication does not transform recklessness into an objective inquiry. Rather, it recognizes the fact that intoxication short of automatism will not deprive an accused of the minimal intent required for this crime.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds intoxication short of automatism won't prevent risk awareness and precluding intoxication defence does not make recklessness objective.

propositions.text: No need to resort to policy considerations to determine intoxication defence availability for s. 434.
propositions.quote: In view of this conclusion, there is no need to resort to policy considerations to determine the availability of the defence of intoxication.

propositions.text: If policy considered, same conclusion would be reached.
propositions.quote: However, had I found it necessary to do so, I would have reached the same conclusion.

paragraphs.summary: The court states policy considerations are unnecessary but would support the conclusion that intoxication defence is unavailable for s. 434.

propositions.text: Section 434 involves damage to property, often associated with alcohol consumption, including this case.
propositions.quote: Section 434 involves damage to property. Damage to property is often associated with alcohol consumption. The present case is no exception.

propositions.text: Allowing intoxication defence would erode policy underlying offence of causing property damage by fire.
propositions.quote: In my view, it would erode the policy underlying the offence of causing damage to property by fire if an accused could rely on self-induced intoxication as a defence.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes s. 434 property damage is often linked to alcohol and allowing intoxication defence would undermine policy.

propositions.text: Trial judge and Court of Appeal erred in characterizing s. 434 as specific intent allowing intoxication defence.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I am respectfully of the view that the trial judge and the majority of the Court of Appeal erred in characterizing s. 434 as a specific intent offence for which the defence of intoxication could be raised.

propositions.text: Properly classified, s. 434 is general intent offence; intoxication short of automatism not considered.
propositions.quote: Properly classified, s. 434 is a general intent offence, meaning that intoxication short of automatism may not be considered.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 434 is a general intent offence and intoxication defence is unavailable, reversing trial judge and Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: Ascertaining intent under s. 434 can be tricky due to varied factual scenarios.
propositions.quote: Leaving aside the question of intoxication, ascertaining whether the intent required under s. 434 has been made out in a particular case can be a tricky exercise.

propositions.text: Trial judge and Court of Appeal noted wide range of factual scenarios under s. 434.
propositions.quote: As the trial judge and the majority of the Court of Appeal noted, there is a wide range of factual scenarios that may arise under s. 434 of the Criminal Code .

propositions.text: Some cases involve direct fire setting; others involve causing object to catch fire leading to property damage.
propositions.quote: Some cases may involve an accused who has set fire directly to the property in issue. Others, like this one, may involve an accused who has caused some object to catch fire, which in turn leads to damage to property.

propositions.text: In direct fire cases, inference of intent or recklessness is ready; in indirect cases, intent assessment may be obtuse.
propositions.quote: In the former, there is typically a ready-made inference that the accused intentionally or recklessly caused damage by fire. In the latter, such an inference may not be so obvious, and the assessment of intent can be obtuse.

propositions.text: Court offers suggestions to triers of fact for deciding intent under s. 434 without setting legal framework.
propositions.quote: Without setting out a legal framework, I offer some suggestions that triers of fact may find helpful in deciding whether the requisite intent has been established.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes intent under s. 434 can be complex with varied scenarios and offers suggestions for triers of fact.

propositions.text: The criminal act in s. 434 is causing damage to property, not setting fire; fire is the mechanism causing damage.
propositions.quote: To begin, it must be remembered that the criminal act in s. 434 is not the setting of a fire. The conduct that has been criminalized is the causing of damage to property. The fire is simply the mechanism by which the damage must be caused.

propositions.text: This distinction between causing damage and setting fire is crucial to intent analysis.
propositions.quote: This distinction is crucial to the analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 434 criminalizes causing property damage, not setting fire, a crucial distinction for intent analysis.

propositions.text: Trier of fact must consider all surrounding circumstances including how fire started in intent assessment.
propositions.quote: In assessing the issue of intent, the trier of fact must of course consider all of the surrounding circumstances. How the fire started is likely to be an important consideration.

propositions.text: Whether fire was set accidentally, negligently, recklessly, or intentionally is important but not dispositive.
propositions.quote: Specifically, was the fire set accidentally, negligently, recklessly, or intentionally? The answer to this question will not be dispositive since, as I have explained, the act of setting a fire is not the conduct that has been criminalized under s. 434 .

propositions.text: How fire started provides important context for intent analysis.
propositions.quote: Nonetheless, it will provide important context for the intent analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court states triers must consider all circumstances including how fire started, which provides important but not dispositive context for intent.

propositions.text: Trier of fact must consider all circumstances to infer if accused intended or was reckless about property damage.
propositions.quote: Deciding how the fire started is only one of the factors a trier of fact may wish to consider. The end game involves looking at all of the surrounding circumstances to determine whether it can be inferred that the accused intended to cause damage to someone else’s property or was reckless whether damage ensued or not.

propositions.text: Intent or recklessness to set fire may not be enough to establish intent or recklessness to cause property damage; context is key.
propositions.quote: The mere fact that the fire was set intentionally or recklessly may not be enough to establish that the accused intentionally or recklessly caused damage to the property. Context is important and will play a key role in determining whether such an inference can be drawn.

propositions.text: Example: controlled fire causing accidental damage does not imply intent or recklessness to damage property.
propositions.quote: Consider, for instance, a homeowner who has started a controlled fire in an outdoor fire pit. If a gust of wind picks up some burning leaves from the fire pit and blows them onto a neighbour’s shed 20 metres away, it does not follow that he intentionally or recklessly damaged the shed.

propositions.text: Despite intentional fire setting, surrounding circumstances may show no intent or recklessness to damage property.
propositions.quote: Notwithstanding his intentional setting of the original fire — namely, the fire in the fire pit — the surrounding circumstances may show that he did not intentionally or recklessly cause damage to the shed: see, e.g., R. v. S.D.D., 2002 NFCA 18, 211 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 157.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains intent to damage property requires context beyond intentional fire setting, citing example where damage was accidental.

propositions.text: In many cases, intentional or reckless fire setting plus circumstances show intent or recklessness to cause property damage.
propositions.quote: In contrast, there are many situations in which an accused has intentionally or recklessly started a fire and the surrounding circumstances make it clear that he or she intended to cause damage to property or was reckless whether damage ensued.

propositions.text: Example: deliberately setting fire to towel and leaving it to burn carpet may infer intent or recklessness to cause damage.
propositions.quote: Take, for instance, a person who has deliberately set fire to a towel. If that person were to drop the towel on the carpet and walk away without making any effort to extinguish the fire, it may be inferred that he or she intended to cause damage to property or was reckless whether damage ensued.

paragraphs.summary: The court gives example where deliberate fire setting and inaction supports inference of intent or recklessness to cause property damage.

propositions.text: Determining guilt under s. 434 depends on intent or recklessness to cause property damage, not how fire was started.
propositions.quote: In summary, the determinative question is not how the fire was started, although the answer to that question may provide important context. An accused’s guilt under s. 434 hinges on whether he or she intentionally or recklessly caused damage to the property in question.

propositions.text: Triers must keep distinction between causing damage and setting fire in mind and examine context and circumstances for intent analysis.
propositions.quote: So long as the trier of fact keeps this important distinction in mind and examines the relevant context and surrounding circumstances, the analysis of intent under s. 434 should be relatively straightforward.

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes that guilt under s. 434 depends on intent or recklessness to cause damage, requiring context and distinction from fire setting.

propositions.text: Trial judge erred in considering intoxication but Crown must show error had material bearing on acquittal for new trial.
propositions.quote: Although I have concluded that the trial judge erred in finding that he could consider Mr. Tatton’s state of intoxication, this does not fully dispose of the appeal. To obtain a new trial, the Crown must demonstrate that the error might reasonably have had a material bearing on the acquittal.

propositions.text: Crown has heavy onus to show error might have materially affected acquittal; abstract possibility insufficient.
propositions.quote: The Crown has a heavy onus. As this Court explained in R. v. Graveline, 2006 SCC 16, [2006] 1 S.C.R. 609, at para. 14: It has been long established, however, that an appeal by the Attorney General cannot succeed on an abstract or purely hypothetical possibility that the accused would have been convicted but for the error of law.

propositions.text: Crown must satisfy appellate court error might reasonably have materially affected acquittal; need not prove verdict would necessarily differ.
propositions.quote: It is the duty of the Crown in order to obtain a new trial to satisfy the appellate court that the error (or errors) of the trial judge might reasonably be thought, in the concrete reality of the case at hand, to have had a material bearing on the acquittal. The Attorney General is not required, however, to persuade us that the verdict would necessarily have been different.

paragraphs.summary: The court states trial judge erred on intoxication but Crown must prove error materially affected acquittal to get new trial, citing Graveline.

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton submits the trial judge based acquittal on accident defence and intoxication had no bearing on verdict
propositions.quote: Mr. Tatton submits that the trial judge based the acquittal on the defence of accident and that intoxication had no bearing on the analysis.

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton argues trial judge's error could not reasonably have affected verdict
propositions.quote: He therefore argues that the trial judge’s error cannot reasonably be thought to have affected the verdict.

propositions.text: Crown argues trial judge considered Mr. Tatton’s intoxication in verdict
propositions.quote: The Crown, on the other hand, argues that the trial judge’s reasons make it clear that he considered Mr. Tatton’s intoxication in arriving at the verdict.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Tatton argues acquittal based on accident defence and intoxication irrelevant; Crown argues trial judge considered intoxication in verdict.

propositions.text: Court accepts Crown's submission that intoxication played material role in outcome
propositions.quote: I accept the Crown’s submission. In my view, when the trial judge’s reasons are read in their entirety, it is apparent that Mr. Tatton’s intoxication played a material role in the outcome.

paragraphs.summary: Court accepts Crown's submission that intoxication materially influenced trial judge's verdict.

propositions.text: Trial judge focused on cause of fire and whether intoxication could be considered
propositions.quote: In his reasons, the trial judge concentrated on the cause of the fire. In particular, the question he posed was whether he could be satisfied that Mr. Tatton intentionally or recklessly started the fire in the frying pan.

propositions.text: Trial judge stated he must determine if intoxication could be considered
propositions.quote: At the outset of his analysis, the trial judge stated that to resolve this issue, he must determine whether Mr. Tatton’s intoxication could be considered.

propositions.text: Trial judge's reasons focus almost exclusively on intoxication issue
propositions.quote: The trial judge’s reasons focus almost exclusively on this issue.

propositions.text: If fire was accidental separate from alcohol role, intoxication analysis was unnecessary
propositions.quote: If, as Mr. Tatton argues, the trial judge concluded that the fire was accidental — separate and apart from any role alcohol may have played — all of this analysis was unnecessary.

propositions.text: It defies logic to suggest acquittal was not influenced by erroneous belief intoxication could be considered
propositions.quote: In my view, it defies logic and common sense to suggest that the trial judge’s decision to acquit was not influenced by his erroneous belief that he could take into account Mr. Tatton’s state of intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds trial judge focused on intoxication in deciding cause of fire and acquittal, making intoxication analysis necessary and influential.

propositions.text: Trial judge's concluding remarks show intoxication was central to reasonable doubt
propositions.quote: The trial judge’s concluding remarks bear this out. In finding that he was left in a state of reasonable doubt, the trial judge stated that one of the questions troubling him was whether Mr. Tatton was “mentally able to carry out such a plan, in view of his drunken condition”

propositions.text: Trial judge did not explicitly find fire accidental but was not satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of intent or recklessness
propositions.quote: Although the trial judge noted Mr. Tatton’s position that the fire was accidental, he did not explicitly make a finding of accident. Rather, he stated that he was not satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Tatton had acted intentionally or recklessly.

propositions.text: Trial judge's reasons imply intoxication caused reasonable doubt about intent
propositions.quote: the clear implication from his reasons is that it was Mr. Tatton’s state of intoxication that left him in a state of reasonable doubt as to whether Mr. Tatton acted with the requisite intent.

propositions.text: Court satisfied test in Graveline has been met
propositions.quote: That being so, I am satisfied that the test in Graveline has been met.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds trial judge's reasons show intoxication caused reasonable doubt about intent, meeting Graveline test.

propositions.text: Court would allow appeal, set aside acquittal, and order new trial
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I would allow the appeal, set aside the acquittal, and order a new trial. Appeal allowed.

propositions.text: Solicitors for appellant, respondent, and intervener named
propositions.quote: Solicitor for the appellant: Attorney General of Ontario, Toronto. Solicitors for the respondent: Gorrell, Greinkie & Rémillard, Morrisburg. Solicitors for the intervener: Kapoor Barristers, Toronto.

propositions.text: Criminal Code now prohibits intoxication to support mistaken belief in consent, consistent with common law
propositions.quote: The Criminal Code now explicitly states that an accused may not rely on intoxication to support his mistaken belief in the complainant’s consent: see s. 273.2 . However, this was the position at common law long before s. 273.2 was enacted (S.C. 1992, c. 38, s. 1): see Leary.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows appeal, orders new trial; solicitor info given; notes Criminal Code and common law on intoxication and consent.
